log/range: A good learning rate could be anywhere from ten to the minus five to ten to the minus one: a range of four factors of ten.
log/uniform: Draw uniformly across that range, and nine draws in ten land between zero point zero one and zero point one. The small rates are barely tried.
log/share: Why? Measured plainly, that one stretch is zero point zero nine long, out of about zero point one for the whole range: nine tenths of it. Everything below zero point zero one shares the last tenth.
log/log: Instead, draw the exponent: u uniform between minus five and minus one, and set the rate to ten to the u.
log/even: Now every decade, every factor of ten, gets the same share of the draws: a quarter each.
log/ex: A u of minus three gives zero point zero zero one. Minus two point five gives ten to the zero point five, about three point one six, times zero point zero zero one: about zero point zero zero three two.
random/grid: Say the learning rate matters a lot, and a second hyperparameter, like the batch size, barely matters. A three by three grid runs nine trainings.
random/waste: But it tries only three learning rates, each three times over.
random/random: Nine random trials try nine different learning rates. When one hyperparameter matters most, random search explores it far better.
judge/train: Each trial is trained on the training split, and judged on the validation split.
judge/pick: Keep the one with the lowest validation loss. Not the lowest training loss: that only rewards memorizing.
judge/test: And leave the test split alone until the very end, so its one number stays honest.
